messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Mina Tran, a 37-year-old married refugee aid worker, came to treatment after months of feeling as if her life had narrowed around one violent afternoon and the years that followed it. She had been stopped outside a detention center while escorting newly arrived families, when a line of police officers pushed the crowd back without warning. Mina remembered the hard slap of a baton against her arm, the crush of bodies, and the moment she realized the officers were not listening to anyone’s pleas. Even now, when she spoke of it, her face tightened with the same terror she said had hit her in that instant. The memory did not come to her as a distant story; it returned with a vivid force that left her overwhelmed and grieving, as if she were again standing in the press of people and hearing herself think that what had happened was deeply unfair and had never been answered.

Since then, certain sights had become potent in ways she found hard to explain to others. Police uniforms on the street, a cluster of cyclists weaving through traffic near her apartment, or a crowded train platform in the city could send her body into alarm before she had time to reason with herself. In those moments Mina would look for the quickest exit, cut conversations short, and begin trying hard not to think about the trauma. She also avoided situations that might make her feel happy or hopeful; after a rare good dinner with her husband, she would feel a pull to cancel the next outing or not let herself savor the evening, as if joy made her vulnerable. What she feared most was that any one of these cues could open the memory again, and once it came she would have to stop what she was doing because the feelings rose so fast and so high.

Mina had come to believe that what happened to her was not only brutal but deeply unfair, and that someone else would not have gotten into this situation. That thought fed her sense that she no longer knew herself; the person who had once been steady in crises now felt unfamiliar to her. It also sharpened her threat monitoring. She found herself watching doorways, scanning faces for authority, and feeling on edge in ordinary settings, especially when the day was busy or unpredictable. At work, where she helped newly resettled families navigate appointments and housing, she began to tense when police were present outside government offices or when a protest passed nearby. The sight of cyclists cutting through a crowded street near the agency could make her stomach drop, and she would move her route or leave early rather than risk the rush of fear that followed.

When the memory returned, it did not only bring terror and grief; it also seemed to confirm her beliefs. Mina would think, again, that the injustice had never been repaired and that no one had really protected her. Those moments drove her back into suppression, and the more she tried to force the memory away, the more it broke through in sharper form. After a crowded commute or an encounter with police near the shelter where she worked, she would spend the evening replaying fragments of the scene and feeling overwhelmed by emotion, then tell herself that if she could just stay busy enough or shut the whole thing out, she might function. Instead, the strain of holding it down seemed to make the image return with even greater force, and she became more convinced that she was not the person she had been before.

To blunt that rising distress, Mina started gambling in the evenings, telling herself she only wanted distraction and a bit of excitement after long days of vigilance. She also sought out risky behavior she would once have avoided, taking too many chances in small but worrying ways, as if the adrenaline briefly interrupted the fear. Yet these strategies left her more unsettled. When she lost money or stayed up too late, she felt worse about herself and more certain that something in her had gone wrong. The shame fed her belief that another person would not have ended up like this, and it deepened the sense of identity loss she already carried. It also made her more irritable at home, with angry outbursts that startled her husband and left her feeling even less like herself.

Over time, the late-night gambling and constant effort to suppress thoughts made sleep difficult. Mina lay awake listening for sirens, and the exhaustion made the world feel more dangerous the next day. On little sleep she became more reactive, more jumpy around authority figures, and quicker to avoid any place that felt crowded or overfull. What began as an attempt to outrun the trauma had become a life organized around its returns, and she finally sought help when she realized she was pulling away from her husband, her work, and any moment that might bring joy. She is frightened that the memory will keep taking over and that she will keep becoming someone she does not recognize, but she is also hoping that treatment might let her feel safe enough to stay present again.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows triggers prompting avoidance and suppression, but does not clearly state that the triggers themselves lead to the maladaptive strategies within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She stopped taking that route to work entirely — better to add twenty minutes to her commute than to feel that way again."
  e.g. "When the anniversary came around, she kept herself moving all day, cleaning, cooking, anything, because sitting still meant the thoughts would catch up."
  e.g. "She started leaving events early, telling herself she was tired, because staying too long meant the chances of something going wrong only multiplied."
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette says cues can open the memory again, but it does not explicitly present the triggers as causing the traumatic memory to occur in a causal way.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The negative appraisals are described as being confirmed by the memory, but there is no paragraph showing negative appraisals driving the memory’s return.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The narrative shows suppression making the image return more forcefully, but not the memory causing the use of maladaptive strategies in a causal chain.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Memory → Threat: The memory brings terror and grief, but the vignette does not clearly state that the memory itself causes an ongoing sense of threat.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette describes threat monitoring and avoidance, but not the sense of threat causing maladaptive strategies in an explicit causal relationship.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not clearly show threat leading to the traumatic memory reoccurring.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: Although she suppresses thoughts, the vignette does not clearly frame maladaptive strategies as causing the memory to return.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows maladaptive strategies worsening shame and self-beliefs, but not a clear causal relation from those strategies to negative appraisals in the required graph sense.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not explicitly show maladaptive strategies increasing the sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Since then, certain sights had become potent in ways she found hard to explain to others.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When Mina saw a police uniform, a cluster of cyclists weaving through traffic, or a crowded train platform, the jolt of alarm sent her straight back to the afternoon outside the detention center; the scene would flood in before she had time to name what was happening, and she would immediately start scanning for the quickest exit and trying not to think about it. After rare good dinners with her husband, even the feeling of hope itself could make her cut the evening short, because staying with anything that felt too open or too good seemed to invite the next surge of fear.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She had come to believe that what happened to her was not only brutal but deeply unfair, and that someone else would not have gotten into this situation.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
That belief kept pulling her back to the memory, as if she needed to replay the moment to understand how she had ended up there and why it had happened to her. The more she told herself that no one should have had to endure it, the more the scene returned in her mind with vivid force.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
When the memory returned, it did not only bring terror and grief; it also seemed to confirm her beliefs.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
When the memory broke through, it made the danger feel immediate again, not like something that had ended but like something still pressing in on her body. The same surge of threat made it harder to hold the scene at a distance, so she found herself trying to shut it down, keep busy, or move away from whatever had brought it close.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
To blunt that rising distress, Mina started gambling in the evenings, telling herself she only wanted distraction and a bit of excitement after long days of vigilance.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
After the memory surfaced, she learned that staying in motion, chasing noise, or taking risks could sometimes crowd it out for a while, so the strategies began to follow the memory automatically. The more she depended on them, the more they seemed to leave the event lodged intact and ready to return.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
To blunt that rising distress, Mina started gambling in the evenings, telling herself she only wanted distraction and a bit of excitement after long days of vigilance.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The fact that she had to keep reaching for distraction and risk made her feel, in a quiet and accumulating way, that she could not cope on her own. Over time, the gambling and other ways of staying away from the memory also convinced her that the threat had never really passed, because her body still behaved as if it had to stay one step ahead.
<<<END>>>
